conversation.content: We'd like you to design a URL shortening service. Think bit.ly scale. Walk us through how you'd approach this.

Before I dive into boxes and arrows, I want to challenge the premise. URL shortening is a feature, not a product. If we're investing engineering resources here, I'd build it as part of a broader developer platform — alongside an API gateway, analytics, and link management. The shortener becomes the entry point into a platform play that has real defensibility.
Interesting framing. Can you elaborate on what this broader platform looks like and how URL shortening fits in?

Think of it as three concentric rings. The core ring is the URL shortening engine — the redirect service, the encoding, the storage. The second ring is the intelligence layer — click analytics, geographic breakdowns, A/B testing on destination URLs, conversion tracking. The third ring is the developer platform — a public API with OAuth, webhooks for link events, SDKs for major languages, and a branded links product for enterprises. bit.ly makes most of its revenue from rings two and three, not ring one.
That's a compelling product vision. Let's ground it in technical requirements. What scale are we designing for?

I'd segment by tier. Free users generate maybe 10M links/day with low read volume. Enterprise customers — the ones that matter for revenue — generate 5M links/day but drive 90% of the read traffic because their links go viral in marketing campaigns. So roughly 15M writes/day — about 175 writes/sec — and maybe 500M reads/day — about 5,800 reads/sec average, but with spikes to 50K during major campaign launches. The real design challenge isn't average load, it's the bursty nature of marketing-driven traffic.
Good segmentation. How does this product-tier thinking influence your architecture decisions?

It fundamentally shapes the multi-tenancy model. Free tier goes through shared infrastructure with aggressive rate limiting — they get best-effort latency. Enterprise customers get dedicated cache pools, priority queuing, and guaranteed SLAs. Architecturally, I'd use a tenant-aware routing layer at the API gateway that inspects the API key, resolves the customer tier, and routes to the appropriate resource pool. This is the same pattern AWS uses for their tiered services — shared compute, isolated resources for premium tiers.
Let's talk about the core redirect service. How do you design for that sub-50ms p99 latency at 50K RPS during spikes?

The redirect path must be ruthlessly optimized — it's the one thing that has to work no matter what. I'd architect it as a completely separate service from the link creation and analytics paths. The redirect service is stateless, deployed at the edge in multiple regions via a CDN partnership or our own PoPs. Each PoP has a local Redis cluster holding the hot set — maybe the top 10M most-accessed links, which is about 5GB of memory. Cache miss goes to a regional database replica. The key insight: for enterprise customers, their links are predictable — we can pre-warm the edge caches when a campaign is created, before any traffic arrives.
Pre-warming is clever. How do you handle the analytics pipeline without impacting redirect latency?

Analytics is a fire-and-forget operation on the redirect path. The edge service writes a click event to a local buffer — a lightweight append-only log — and returns the redirect immediately. A local agent ships these events to Kafka in micro-batches every 100ms. From Kafka, we fork into two streams: a real-time path using Flink for live dashboards that enterprise customers pay premium for, and a batch path into S3/Parquet for the deep analytics — geographic breakdowns, device distribution, time-series analysis. The real-time path gives sub-second visibility; the batch path powers the BI features at much lower cost per query.
You mentioned this is a developer platform. Tell me about the API design and how you'd make it extensible.

The API is the product for developers. I'd design it as a RESTful API with resource-oriented URLs, but also offer a GraphQL endpoint for the analytics queries where clients need flexibility. Core resources: links, domains, campaigns, and analytics. Every link creation returns a link object with embedded analytics URLs, following HATEOAS principles. For extensibility: webhooks for link events — created, clicked, expired — so developers can build workflows. A JavaScript SDK for the most common use case: embedding tracking links in web apps. Rate limits and quotas are communicated via standard headers. The key differentiator: deep link support for mobile apps, QR code generation, and smart redirects based on device type — these are features that make developers choose us over rolling their own.
How would you handle custom branded domains — like links.nike.com pointing to your service?

Branded domains are the highest-margin feature in this business — enterprises will pay $50K/year for this. Technically, the customer creates a CNAME record pointing their subdomain to our edge. We run an automated TLS certificate provisioning pipeline using Let's Encrypt or a commercial CA — when a new domain is added, we trigger certificate issuance, validate via DNS challenge, and deploy the cert to all edge PoPs within minutes. The routing layer needs a domain-to-tenant mapping in a fast lookup store — this is another Redis use case. The tricky part is certificate renewal at scale — with 10K custom domains, we need a robust cert lifecycle manager that handles renewals 30 days before expiry, with alerting for DNS misconfigurations.
Let's talk about data strategy. You mentioned analytics is a differentiator. How do you think about the data architecture holistically?

The data architecture has three stores optimized for different access patterns. First, the link metadata store — this is PostgreSQL sharded by tenant_id, not link_id, because most queries are tenant-scoped. Second, the click event store — this is a columnar store like ClickHouse, partitioned by date and tenant_id, optimized for time-range aggregation queries. Third, the real-time counters — Redis with sorted sets for trending links and HyperLogLog for unique visitor counts. The strategic insight: click data is our moat. The more data we collect, the better our analytics product becomes, and the harder it is for customers to leave. We should invest in data retention — keep raw events for 2 years for enterprise, roll up to daily aggregates after 90 days for free tier. This data also enables us to build predictive features down the road — link performance prediction, optimal posting time recommendations.
What about abuse prevention? Short URLs are notoriously used for phishing and malware distribution.

This is a trust and safety problem that can kill the product if handled poorly. Google Safe Browsing and similar services will flag your entire domain if too many malicious links originate from it. My approach is multi-layered. At creation time: scan the destination URL against known malware/phishing databases, run heuristic checks for suspicious patterns, and require CAPTCHA for unauthenticated creation. Post-creation: periodically re-scan destinations because pages can change, implement a user reporting mechanism, and use ML to detect patterns — bulk creation from similar IPs targeting financial institutions, for example. For response: immediate link deactivation with an interstitial warning page, and proactive reporting to Safe Browsing. Organizationally, this needs a dedicated trust and safety team with SLAs — a flagged link should be reviewed within 15 minutes during business hours.
How do you think about the organizational structure to build and operate this platform?

I'd organize around the three rings I mentioned. Team one: Core Infrastructure — owns the redirect service, encoding, storage layer, and SLA for redirect latency. This is a small, senior team — maybe 5 engineers — because the core service should be stable and rarely change. Team two: Intelligence Platform — owns analytics pipeline, real-time processing, data warehouse, and the customer-facing analytics product. Larger team, maybe 8-10, because this is where most feature development happens. Team three: Developer Platform — owns API gateway, authentication, SDKs, documentation, and developer relations. Maybe 6 engineers plus a DevRel person. Cross-cutting: an SRE team that sets reliability standards and incident response across all three. Each team owns their services end-to-end, including on-call.
What's your competitive analysis? How does this platform compete with existing players?

The market has three segments. Consumer/free — dominated by bit.ly and tinyurl, low margin, high volume. Enterprise link management — bit.ly Enterprise and Branch.io, high margin. Developer tools — relatively underserved. I'd initially target the developer tools segment — offer a generous free tier with great docs and SDKs, monetize through usage-based pricing on analytics and custom domains. The wedge is developer experience — if our API is 10x easier to integrate than bit.ly's, we win the developer segment. Then we expand upmarket into enterprise with features like SSO, team management, and audit logs. The key metric isn't link volume — it's API integration count and monthly active developers.
Let's come back to technical depth. How would you handle a multi-region deployment for global latency?

For the redirect service, I'd deploy in at least 5 regions — US East, US West, Europe, Singapore, and Sao Paulo — covering the major traffic centers. Each region runs an independent redirect stack: load balancer, redirect service, local Redis cache, and a read replica of the link database. Writes are centralized in the primary region — US East — since link creation is much lower volume and doesn't need ultra-low latency. The DNS layer uses latency-based routing to send users to the nearest PoP. For consistency, I accept eventual consistency on the read path — a new link might take 2-3 seconds to propagate globally via async replication, which is fine because there's a natural delay between link creation and first click. For the analytics pipeline, each region runs a local Kafka cluster that ships events to a central data warehouse — this keeps analytics latency low without cross-region writes on the hot path.
What's the cost model look like? How do you think about unit economics?

Let me model this. The redirect service is the biggest cost center — 500M requests/day across 5 regions. At roughly $0.01 per 10K requests for compute, that's about $500/day or $180K/year for compute. Storage grows at 15M links/day — at 500 bytes each, that's about 2.7TB/year, maybe $100/year in S3. The expensive part is analytics — storing and processing 500M click events daily in ClickHouse and Kafka costs roughly $300K/year. Edge infrastructure with custom domains and TLS: maybe $200K/year. Total infrastructure: roughly $700K/year. If we have 100 enterprise customers at $50K/year average, that's $5M ARR — a healthy 86% gross margin. The free tier is a customer acquisition cost: subsidized by enterprise revenue. This is a high-margin SaaS business if we nail the enterprise conversion funnel.
Final question: what are the biggest risks to this platform, and how would you mitigate them?

Three major risks. First, domain reputation — if our domains get flagged by browsers or email providers, our core value proposition dies. Mitigation: invest heavily in abuse prevention, maintain relationships with Safe Browsing teams, and encourage custom domains so customers aren't dependent on our shared domain. Second, concentration risk — if one enterprise customer drives 40% of traffic, a contract loss could require rapid scale-down. Mitigation: usage-based pricing that aligns costs with revenue, and committed-use contracts for large customers. Third, technology commoditization — Cloudflare Workers can build a URL shortener in 50 lines of code. Our defense is the analytics and developer platform moat, not the redirect technology. If we don't build that moat fast enough, we're competing on price against hyperscalers. I'd fund the analytics roadmap aggressively in year one.
Excellent. You brought a very strategic lens to what could have been a straightforward system design question. Thank you for your time.

strengths: Exceptional product and platform vision — reframed a commodity feature into a defensible platform business
Strong unit economics analysis with concrete cost modeling and margin calculations
Thoughtful organizational design aligned with the technical architecture
weaknesses: Could have explored failure scenarios and disaster recovery in more depth
Didn't discuss database migration strategy or schema evolution for the growing platform
